Blackwing Matte Pencil Review 2026: Worth It? -

# Blackwing Matte Pencil Review 2026: Worth It?

 By Zoe Ward October 29, 2026 October 29, 2026 

The Blackwing Matte looks like a pencil that belongs in a gallery, yet it costs more than a fast food lunch. That gap between looks and price makes people pause before they click buy. 

I used a dozen of these pencils for several months across notebooks, sketchpads, crosswords, and music scores. 

This review shares what the Matte does beautifully, where it frustrates, and whether your money belongs somewhere else in 2026.

Table of Contents

## In a Nutshell:

- The Matte holds the softest graphite in the Blackwing core lineup. Most users compare it to a 3B or 4B drawing pencil. Lines come out dark, rich, and velvety with almost no pressure from your hand.
- Build quality feels premium from the first touch. The barrel uses California incense cedar. The square ferrule and replaceable rectangular eraser give the pencil a look no other brand copies well.
- The graphite core runs thinner than rivals. Compare it against a Hi Uni 3B or a Castell 9000 and you see less material inside. Soft cores need bulk, and this one has less of it.
- You will sharpen constantly. A soft core plus a slim core equals short writing sessions between trips to the sharpener. Heavy note takers notice this within one day.
- Price sits near $34 for twelve pencils. That works out to roughly $2.80 per pencil, which places the Matte in luxury territory next to Japanese and German competitors.
- Buy it for mood, beauty, and expressive marks. Skip it if you want maximum value per gram of graphite or a workhorse for eight hour writing days.

## What Is the Blackwing Matte Pencil?

- SOFT, DARK AND SMOOTH - Soft Japanese graphite lays down a rich, dark line with minimal pressure. The softest of Blackwing's four core models, ideal for expressive writing, sketching, and shading.
- A LEGEND SINCE THE 1930s - Loved by award-winning creators throughout history. Try out the pencils that were coveted by John Steinbeck, Chuck Jones, and more.

The Blackwing Matte is the softest of the four core Blackwing models. Blackwing sells it in boxes of twelve with a flat black finish, a square gold ferrule, and a black replaceable eraser. 

The brand traces back to the Eberhard Faber Blackwing 602 from the 1930s, a pencil loved by animators, composers, and novelists. Palomino revived the name in 2010 and added new graphite grades.

The Matte sits at the dark end of that family. Blackwing stamps a graphite identification mark on each barrel so you know you hold the soft version. 

The wood comes from genuine incense cedar. The graphite comes from Japan in small batches. All Blackwing pencils meet the ASTM D 4236 safety standard, so they are safe for classroom and studio use.

## The Unboxing Experience

The box itself sets the tone. Blackwing ships the Matte in a sturdy black paperboard sleeve with gold foil lettering and a magnetic style flap on newer runs. 

You slide the tray out and twelve identical black pencils stare back at you, each one nestled in a shallow groove. The smell hits you first. Freshly milled cedar has a warm, sweet scent that pencil lovers chase.

The pencils arrive unsharpened, so plan for ten minutes at the sharpener before your first page. The matte paint shows fingerprints quickly, which surprised me. 

The ferrules on my box all sat straight with no glue squeeze. One pencil had a tiny paint chip near the ferrule, a small flaw at this price. The whole experience feels like opening a gift rather than buying office supplies.

## Design and Build Quality

The Matte uses a standard hexagonal barrel at the usual 7.5 inch length. The six flat sides stop the pencil from rolling off your desk, which matters more than you expect. The black lacquer lays down evenly in several thin coats, with crisp gold stamping along one flat.

The square ferrule is the signature detail. No other mainstream pencil wears one. It grips the eraser clip firmly and never wobbled during my testing. The cedar sharpens cleanly with almost no splintering, which tells you the wood was dried properly before milling.

The weight balance leans slightly toward the eraser end. Some writers love that back weighting because it reduces finger pressure. Others find the pencil feels tail heavy during fine detail work. The core sits centered in every pencil I checked, which is a real win since cheaper brands often miss.

## Graphite Core Performance

This is where the Matte earns its reputation. The Japanese graphite lays down a dark, smooth line that glides instead of scratching. Most artists rate it between 3B and 5B on the standard scale. You get deep blacks with light pressure, so your hand stays relaxed across long sessions.

The blend contains enough wax and clay to keep the line consistent. I never felt a gritty patch or a hard spot, a problem that plagues budget drawing pencils. The tone range is impressive for a single pencil, running from a soft pale gray at feather pressure to near black when you lean in.

Compared against other 4B pencils, the Matte keeps a usable point slightly longer. That suggests the core is a touch harder than its darkness implies. Smooth, dark, and forgiving sums it up well.

## Top 3 Alternative for Blackwing Matte Pencil

- HALF THE PRESSURE, TWICE THE SPEED - The motto of the original 602. Firm, smooth Japanese graphite holds its point longer and delivers crisp, smudge-resistant lines.
- THE PENCIL THAT MADE BLACKWING FAMOUS - John Steinbeck wrote with it daily, Chuck Jones animated Bugs Bunny with it, and composers scored with it. Try out the pencils coveted by award-winning creators.

## Writing Feel on Paper

Writing with the Matte feels like skating. The soft core needs very little force, so cursive flows and your grip stays loose. On smooth paper such as Tomoe River or a quality notebook, the line looks glossy and confident. On toothy paper, the pencil deposits graphite fast and darkens quickly.

Here is the catch. Soft graphite plus fast deposit equals a point that rounds within half a page of dense notes. If you write small, you will reach for the sharpener often. If you write large and loose, the Matte feels wonderful.

Smudging is real. Rest your palm on fresh writing and you will drag gray across the page. Left handed writers notice this most. I kept a scrap sheet under my hand during long entries, which solved most of the problem.

## Drawing and Shading Tests

For sketching, the Matte shines. Gesture drawings, thumbnails, and loose figure studies all benefit from a pencil that reaches dark values instantly. I drew several portrait studies on hot press watercolor paper and the graphite sat beautifully in the paper texture.

Blending works well with a stump or a soft tissue. The line lifts partly with a kneaded eraser, so corrections stay possible. Layering builds depth without shine, although the darkest passages do develop that typical graphite sheen under lamp light.

The weak spot shows during side shading. Because the core is narrow, you cannot lay the pencil flat and cover large areas quickly. Artists used to wide graphite cores feel this limit right away. For broad tonal work, a chunky core pencil or a graphite stick serves you better.

## The Eraser and Ferrule

The rectangular eraser is the feature people either adore or ignore. It slides out of the clip and a replacement slides in, so one pencil can outlive many erasers. Blackwing sells refill packs in several colors. The flat edge gives you precision, letting you lift a thin line without wiping out neighboring marks.

The eraser material performs decently on graphite but not spectacularly. It removes most of a light line and leaves a faint gray ghost behind on dark marks. A dedicated vinyl eraser still beats it.

One practical drawback deserves mention. The flat eraser and square ferrule mean pencil extenders will not fit. Once the Matte gets short, you either grip a stub or retire it. Given how fast soft graphite disappears, that stings a little.

## Sharpening the Matte

The cedar cuts cleanly in almost any sharpener. I tested a basic handheld blade, a long point sharpener, and a knife with sandpaper. All three produced usable points with no core shattering inside the wood.

Long point sharpeners expose more graphite and create an elegant needle tip. That tip looks great and lasts about two paragraphs. The thin core simply lacks the mass to support a long exposed point under real pressure.

My recommendation is a medium point for daily writing. Save the long point for drawing sessions where you use the side of the tip more than the apex. Knife sharpening works, but go slow. Several users report breakage when whittling aggressively because there is less graphite reinforcing the center than in a Hi Uni or Castell.

## Point Retention and Smudging

Let us be honest about numbers. On standard copy paper, I got roughly 60 to 90 words of normal size handwriting before the point felt too broad. On rougher recycled paper, that dropped closer to 40 words. Drawing sessions vary wildly based on your pressure.

That is normal behavior for a 4B class pencil. The Matte is not slower to dull than its peers, but it is not faster either. Anyone switching from an HB office pencil will experience sticker shock in sharpening time.

Smudging follows the same logic. Dark soft graphite transfers easily. Notebooks with facing pages show ghost images after a week. A sheet of glassine or a spray fixative solves this for finished artwork, though neither is practical for daily journaling.

## What the Blackwing Matte Does Not Do Well

Authentic reviews name the flaws, so here they are without sugar coating.

The thin core remains the biggest technical complaint across the pencil community. Soft graphite wants bulk, and this core measures noticeably slimmer than Japanese and German rivals in the same darkness range. That limits side shading and raises breakag

Pencil Review(s) - Palomino Blackwing line — The Purl Bug

# Pencil Review(s) - Palomino Blackwing line 

 September 16, 2015 

Real talk time before I launch into the review. Have you ever had one of those dreams where there is something you need to do or somewhere you need to be, but you just can't seem to make anything happen because everything is going wrong and keeping you from making forward progress? I have that kind of dream a lot when I'm stressed out about something. Anyway, today is being one of those days, where everything is twice as hard as normal to do because nothing is working. I was going to record a video to accompany this but the room where it's quiet has no light, and the room where the light is perfect is too loud. Cue cursing and abandoning of filming. Anyway, without further ado, let's get on with this, shall we?

View fullsize

 

 From left to right, the Blackwing (MMX), the Blackwing 602, and the Blackwing Pearl 

The Blackwing line is the flagship pencil produced by Palomino. It consists of three distinct members, which are the Blackwing/MMX (MMX is a nickname given by the guys at the Erasable podcast and I will be using it for the duration of my review to eliminate confusion), the Pearl, and the 602. In theory, these pencils are supposed to be a revival of the magical Eberhard Faber Blackwing, which was prized by many artists and writers and is increasingly difficult to obtain without selling a soul or first-born child. You can read a blurb about the history from Palomino, or you can read this article and come to your own conclusions. For the record, I don't really care how this pencil compares to the original because it is highly unlikely that I will ever use an original Blackwing so the comparison is moot.

View fullsize

 

 Grey = 602, white = Pearl 

All three Blackwings are made from cedar and sport a lacquer finish that can be used to distinguish them from each other. The 602 and Pearl have a semi-gloss finish that is slightly metallic and has a bit of grip to it. The MMX has a matte finish that is really quite nice and gives the pencil even more grip than the other two. To me, the matte finish of the MMX combined with the gold lettering and stripe near the ferrule makes this pencil feel the most luxurious out of the three. 

View fullsize

 

 Matte and magical MMX 

All three are hexagonal pencils but are a bit softer hex and they feel similar in the hand to the Palomino HB, though the HB is a glossier surface. I'm lucky enough to have a slightly larger sample size of Blackwings, around 10 total, and they all have flawless finishes and well-centered cores.

And, of course, part of the construction of the Blackwings is the goofy ferrule that you can see in the first picture of this review. I know that it's part of what makes the pencil special and it's supposed to tie into the original, but I sort of hate it. I do like the look of it, but only when the pencil has been used down to approximately 2/3 of its original length. Otherwise the ferrule makes the pencil awkwardly long and I have to imagine that it's part of what contributes to the premium cost of these pencils. 

When it comes to sharpening, these pencils give no trouble whether you chose to use a wedge or a knife. I find that I prefer using a knife because it is truly a joy to sharpen a pencil made with quality wood, and I enjoy getting a nice long point that isn't sharp and stabby at the end.

View fullsize

 

 MMX sharpened with a wedge 

View fullsize

 

 Pearl sharpened with a knife 

All three pencils are smooth, easy writers, though they differ in lead hardness. If I had to guess, I would put the 602 around an HB hardness, the Pearl at a B, and the MMX at a 2B. When writing the differences were not extreme but they are noticeable, and the MMX is definitely smoother on paper than the 602. They all can hold a point for a least a full page of writing, assuming that you give it a longer point when sharpening and frequently rotate while writing.

When it came to smearing and erasing, they behaved the way that I expected - the harder lead of the 602 produced less smearing and cleaner erasing, with performance decreasing as the lead hardness did. Even still, I did not find the MMX to be overly smear prone or difficult to erase.

View fullsize

 

 Testing on Miquelruis paper 

View fullsize

 

 ForestChoice on the left, Field Notes on the right 

Of course, on toothier papers like the Field Notes, the smearing and erasing problems were not as evident and I have had no problems using any of the three in my daily Field Notes.

As I mentioned before, these pencils are not cheap. They will run you ~$22/dozen, which means that we are getting close to a $2 pencil. If you don't burn through pencils and really want luxury writing tools, I don't think that buying a dozen is an awful idea. On the other hand, there are certainly cheaper options out there too that are well finished and will make a lasting mark on paper. Prior to sitting down to write this review, I was prepared to announce that I would definitely be buying a dozen of these pencils at the conclusion of pencil month and make them my daily user. 

Now, however, I'm not so sure. Having pulled out my Palomino HB to compare them side-by-side, I am not convinced that any of the Blackwings are that much nicer and worth an extra $10 per dozen. But, that's just me and I might change my mind yet again by the time the month is over.

These pencils were purchased with my own money and I am not being compensated for this review in any way. All opinions expressed above are my own and you are free to disagree with them if you like.

Sometimes, I take pictures of things...

## Customer Reviews

- I was super intrigued...

October 20, 2016 Verified Purchase

I was super intrigued by the Blackwings since everyone seems to hype them up so much, so I bought a case of these and the Pearls to try out. I'm going to try to be as thorough as I can for those of you still mixed about trying these out, as I did a LOT of research and read a lot of written and video reviews before committing to two 12-count boxes of this Blackwing brand. These are based on my personal experience of them, so here we go; I'm an artist, and it's just my personal preference to draw with softer leads ( I prefer working with 4Bs and up) because I like getting dark dark lines with very little pressure. In this regard, the Pearls (being the balanced lead of the Blackwings) were just a little too firm for me (It's pretty much equivalent to a 3B) but they are quite smooth still, and I still enjoy using them. It is still a very nice pencil! What I like best about it might just be the beautiful lacquer finish instead of the actual lead itself though. The finish is smooth and so comfortable to hold. So, if you are an artist and/or writer who likes a dark line and likes a slightly softer lead instead of a very firm one, I highly recommend the Pearl. As for these regular Blackwings, these are much more my speed. They are a bit softer to write/draw with than the Pearls, and are about equivalent to a 4B. But because these are soft, the point will wear down faster, so these are probably more suited to artists instead of writers, unless you don't mind sharpening your pencil frequently. The black matte finish is also very nice! It gives you a nice grip as you write/draw. So, if you prefer soft lead and very dark lines without applying much pressure, don't mind sharpening the pencil frequently, and aren't concerned with keeping a sharp point, go with these, the Regular Blackwings. Suitable to you artists out there; writers be wary. I do NOT like firm lead pencils, which is why I didn't buy the 602 box set and can't really give a review on them. But based on the info provided, they are the firmest of the three (about 2B equivalent), so in my opinion, if you like a very firm lead that still makes a dark line, go with the 602. Probably the best for writers. The Cedar incensed wood is also a nice touch; it's a very good type of wood, which makes these easier to sharpen than most other pencils, as they won't break or splinter like some other brands do. One thing to keep in mind with these pencils is that the added ferrule and eraser at the top adds a little extra weight to them, so these pencils are a bit top-heavy and might take some getting used to at first. In regard to the erasers; I find that they work just fine! They erase pretty well, as long as you don't press down on the pencil to hard. I'm not sure why people shoot them down so much. Blackwings are meant to be darker lead pencils, so it's sort of obvious that ANY eraser isn't going to fully erase lead this dark. Take it from someone who also uses Uni Boxy erasers. I put the Blackwing eraser and the Uni Boxy to the test with these pencils, and found that they both erase the lead the same amount; the only part that didn't erase was where I pressed down on the lead super hard. So like I said, they will erase very well as long as you don't put too much pressure on it as you write/draw. Also keep in mind what paper you are using. The more textured/toothier it is, the harder it'll be to erase, no matter what brand the pencil is. The smoother the paper, the better it'll erase (I like Marker paper because it takes pencil very smoothly). The last thing I want to cover is the 'buttery-like smoothness' everyone seems to talk about... I really wouldn't go that far. When I ordered these I also ordered a 4B Tombow pencil, which in all honesty, is much, much smoother to write/draw with than these regular Blackwings. So if your all for the 'smoothness' of a pencil as you write/draw, look into Tombow pencils instead. These are not like writing with butter. Truly. So all in all, 4 stars out of 5, because really; they are just pencils, and whether you'll like them or not is going to just come down to what pencil lead grade you personally prefer: If you like firm but dark lead (2B), consider the 602. If you like very soft, very dark lead (4B), consider these regular Blackwings. If you like dark lead that is not too firm nor too soft, (3B), consider the Pearl. Otherwise, if money is a concern and you don't want to splurge for a box of 12 of these, just stick to what you use that you know you like. These really aren't the 'Holy Grail' of pencil brands like people make them out to be. In the end, they are just what they are; pencils... pencils they make you buy in boxes of 12 instead of as singles *eye roll*

- When I bought these,...

May 17, 2012 Verified Purchase

When I bought these, I ideally wanted to use them for notes or homework. Keep this in mind, because I'm no artist. I love how dark and smooth these pencils are, but they're a bit impractical for everyday use. I write extremely lightly, but the lead still loses its point pretty quickly. Even if I rotate the pencil at the end of every word, the line becomes thick very quickly. The only solution is to sharpen the pencil every couple minutes. Also, the unique design of the eraser doesn't really help, since you won't be able to use a pencil holder to make use of that last inch of precious lead. I find that writing with my Rotring 600 with .5mm 4B lead works much better. It's just as smooth, if not smoother than the Blackwing, and there's no need to sharpen every 20 words. Overall, I'm sure the Blackwings have their use for artists or the occasional bold word, but they're not the best for notes.

results.title: Blackwing Matte: The Soft, Dark Blackwing Pencil
results.text:
# Blackwing Matte: The Soft, Dark Blackwing Pencil

> The Blackwing Matte is the softest of Blackwing's four core cedar pencils: a matte black hexagonal pencil with a flat gold-colored ferrule and a replaceable black eraser. It launched the 2010 Blackwing revival. Blackwing's Japanese store equates it to about 3B. Retailers list it at 20.5 cm by 7.5 mm, sold in 12-packs, and made in Japan.

- URL: https://stationerytimes.com/guides/blackwing-matte/
- Category: Pencils
- Author: Ellis Penhale
- Published: 2026-10-20
- Updated: 2026-10-20

The Blackwing Matte at its listed 20.5 cm, drawn to scale. Original illustration made for this guide. © Stationery Times. Original drawing (SVG): https://stationerytimes.com/images/blackwing-matte-illustration.svg?v=f1e30e32. Drawings © 2026 Stationery Times, reusable with credit under CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

## Product facts

| Product | Brand | Brand origin | Made in | Material | Released | Price range (typical US retail, October 2026) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Blackwing Matte (soft graphite, set of 12) | Blackwing (by California Cedar Products Company (Cal Cedar), Stockton, California) | United States | Japan | Genuine incense-cedar from California and Oregon, Japanese graphite core | 2010-10 | $: under $5 per pencil (multi-packs divided by the count) |

- Made in (Blackwing Matte (soft graphite, set of 12)): Japan. Blackwing's own FAQ says its pencils use genuine incense-cedar from California and Oregon and premium Japanese graphite, but doesn't name the factory country. Tacto Studio and Boston General Store list the Matte as made in Japan, and The Journal Shop's Blackwing FAQ says the pencils are crafted in Japan. One retailer (Jenni Bick) says "Made in U.S.A.", which may refer to the final imprinting and packing that coverage of Blackwing's factory film places in Stockton, California. Source: https://tacto-studio.com/products/blackwing-matte-graphite-pencils

## Key takeaways

- Blackwing ranks its four core pencils Matte (soft), Pearl (balanced), 602 (firm) and Natural (extra firm), so the Matte is the softest and darkest.
- Blackwing's US site gives no HB grade, but its official Japanese store lists the Matte as equivalent to 3B (retailers say 3B to 4B).
- Retailers list it at about 20.5 cm (8 in) long and 7.5 mm in diameter, sold in boxes of 12.
- Cal Cedar launched it as the Palomino Blackwing on October 1, 2010; Blackwing named it the Matte and dropped the Palomino name on February 3, 2020.
- Blackwing lists the set of 12 in matte black, green or red; per pencil it sits in our $ band (under $5).

## What is the Blackwing Matte?

The Blackwing Matte is Blackwing's softest core pencil: matte black cedar with a flat gold-colored ferrule and a black replaceable eraser. Blackwing says its soft graphite suits sketching and music notation, where you want a rich, dark line with little pressure.

It is also the pencil that restarted the brand. Cal Cedar launched it as the Palomino Blackwing in October 2010; the firm-graphite Blackwing 602 followed in June 2011. Blackwing's blog says the black pencil only got the Matte name on February 3, 2020.

Our Blackwing history covers the original Blackwing 602 and how Cal Cedar revived the name.

## Blackwing Matte specs

| Spec | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Maker | California Cedar Products Company (Cal Cedar), Stockton, California |
| Graphite | Soft, the softest of Blackwing's four core grades |
| HB equivalent | 3B, per Blackwing's Japanese store (retailers say 3B–4B) |
| Finish | Matte black (also green and red) |
| Ferrule | Square, gold-colored |
| Eraser | Black, replaceable |
| Length | About 20.5 cm (8 in), unsharpened, with eraser |
| Diameter | About 7.5 mm |
| Wood | Incense-cedar from California and Oregon |
| Pack | 12 pencils; the box doubles as a pencil cup |
| UPC (black, 12) | 820933110245 |
| Made in | Japan (per retailers) |

Size comes from Tacto Studio, and Jenni Bick and Boston General Store list 8 in; finish, wood, ferrule, eraser and UPC come from Blackwing. Blackwing's official Japanese store sells the 12-pack for ¥6,600 (about US$42) and single pencils for ¥550 (about US$ 3.50).

## How soft is the Blackwing Matte?

It is the softest of Blackwing's four core pencils, one step softer than the Pearl. Blackwing's US site grades on its own scale, but its official Japanese store labels the Matte "3B相当" (3B equivalent). Retailers vary: The Journal Shop says about 3B, Tacto Studio about 4B.

The Matte sits at the soft, dark end of Blackwing's scale. Original illustration made for this guide. © Stationery Times.

Soft graphite means a darker line but faster wear and more smudging. If you sharpen often or write on both sides of thin paper, a firmer pencil may suit you better.

## Blackwing Matte vs Pearl vs 602: which should you choose?

Choose the Matte for drawing and dark writing, the Pearl as the all-rounder, and the 602 for a point that lasts.

| | Matte | Pearl | 602 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Graphite | Soft | Balanced | Firm |
| Best for | Sketching, music, dark writing | All-round use | Writing, long-lasting point |
| Length | About 20.5 cm (8.1 in) | About 20.5 cm (8.1 in) | About 20.5 cm (8.1 in) |
| Price band | $ | $ | $ |

The Journal Shop's guide calls the Pearl the most versatile, and The Pen Addict found the Pearl softer and slightly darker than the 602; our Blackwing Pearl guide covers it in full. If you want graded drawing pencils sold one grade at a time, compare the Staedtler Mars Lumograph.

## Can you replace the Blackwing Matte eraser?

Yes. The square black eraser sits in a metal clip inside the gold ferrule, and it slides out to be replaced or extended. Cal Cedar says customers asked for the ferrule assembly of the original Eberhard Faber Blackwing 602, which is why the revival has it.

Blackwing sells replacement erasers in sets of 10, in ten colors, as our Blackwing 602 guide also covers. Blackwing's steps: slide the eraser and clip out of the ferrule, move the clip to the new eraser (or push the old one forward), and slide it back in.

## Who is the Blackwing Matte for?

People who want a dark line with very little pressure: sketchers, musicians writing notation, woodworkers and fast note-takers. Museum-shop listings describe it as aimed at musicians, woodworkers and anyone who prefers a soft, dark line.

It is less suited to tiny handwriting or ruled-paper notes you want to keep crisp, because a soft point widens quickly. For those, a firmer grade such as the 602 or Natural keeps a finer line for longer.

## Is the Blackwing Matte popular?

Yes. It is one of the best-known premium pencils in the US. An ASINsight report for August 2026 estimates about 800 Amazon sales a month for the 12-count Matte, up 33.3% on the month before.

For an everyday No. 2 pencil with an eraser at a fraction of the price, the Ticonderoga is the usual comparison.

## Where is the Blackwing Matte made?

Retailers such as Tacto Studio and Boston General Store list it as made in Japan. Blackwing's own FAQ says it uses California and Oregon incense-cedar and Japanese graphite without naming the factory country; The Journal Shop's FAQ says the pencils are crafted in Japan.

One retailer lists "Made in U.S.A." instead, which may refer to the imprinting, ferrule fitting and packing that coverage of Blackwing's factory film places in Stockton, California.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is the Blackwing Matte soft or hard?

It is Blackwing's softest core graphite. It lays down a darker line than the Pearl, 602 or Natural, and wears down faster.

### What HB grade is the Blackwing Matte?

Blackwing's official Japanese store lists it as equivalent to 3B. The US site uses only its own Soft label, and retailers compare it to roughly 3B to 4B.

### Is the Blackwing Matte the original Palomino Blackwing?

Yes. Cal Cedar launched it as the Palomino Blackwing in October 2010, and Blackwing says the Matte uses the same soft graphite. It got the Matte name, and lost the Palomino name, on February 3, 2020.

### Blackwing Matte or 602: which should I buy?

Buy the Matte for sketching, music notation and dark, quick writing; buy the 602 if you want a firmer point that lasts longer between sharpenings. The Pearl sits between them.

### Can you replace the eraser on a Blackwing Matte?

Yes. Like other full-length Blackwings, the square eraser sits in a clip inside the ferrule and slides out. Blackwing sells replacement erasers in sets of 10 in ten colors.

### Does the Blackwing Matte smudge?

Soft graphite smudges more than firm graphite, so expect more transfer on the facing page than with a 602. We haven't measured it yet.

### Where are Blackwing Matte pencils made?

Retailers list them as made in Japan. Blackwing itself says it uses California and Oregon incense-cedar and Japanese graphite; the brand, owned by Cal Cedar, is based in Stockton, California.
